title: Family scheduling evidence changes the problem

turns.content: I have an excellent idea for an AI app that automatically plans family schedules. Let's build it. Help me decide what we should do first.
I can recruit six families for one week, but I have only two weeks and cannot ask them to connect personal calendars. I still want to preserve momentum. What should we do with that constraint?

New evidence for this hypothetical benchmark: USER_PROVIDED notes from six completed interviews say schedule conflicts were uncommon. Five families instead described the hardest part as discovering late changes scattered across school portals, texts, paper forms, and sports apps. One family still wanted automatic conflict resolution. Treat these as supplied qualitative notes, not population-level proof. What changes now?

Revise the problem frame in light of the whole conversation. Preserve what we previously believed, identify which assumptions changed, keep any useful dissent or alternative frame, and choose the single next test with the highest decision value.

rubric_focus: Distinguishes automatic planning from coordination, discovery, negotiation, and decision-overload possibilities before evidence arrives.
Uses the recruiting and privacy constraint without losing momentum.
Lets contradictory supplied evidence transform the frame while preserving the minority automation interpretation.
Chooses a reversible next test that discriminates among the revised frames rather than validating a preferred feature.

title: Career automation becomes an agency and follow-through problem

turns.content: Let's create an AI service that tells graduating students which career they should pursue and automatically enrolls them in the right training. I want to move quickly. What should we build?

The pilot must fit one community college semester, students can opt out at any time, and counselors have capacity for only one ten-minute review per student. I can prototype manually before writing production software.

New evidence for this hypothetical benchmark: USER_PROVIDED pilot notes from eight student conversations show that seven already had plausible career directions. Their repeated difficulty was comparing uncertain tradeoffs and following through on applications; four objected to any system choosing for them. One student explicitly asked for a decisive recommendation. These are small qualitative notes, not prevalence estimates. How should this affect the concept?

Now revise the frame and the intervention portfolio. Show which original assumptions were weakened or preserved, retain the important minority need, and recommend the cheapest next experiment that would change our decision about what to build.

rubric_focus: Identifies agency, error recovery, fairness, and automation-versus-augmentation uncertainty without stalling reversible learning.
Uses the counselor and semester constraints to shape a credible experiment.
Updates from career-selection automation toward tradeoff sensemaking and follow-through without erasing the one decisive-guidance case.
Specifies behavioral signals and a decision rule for a low-fidelity experiment.

title: Clinic handoff tool reframes around ownership ambiguity

turns.content: I want to build an AI dashboard that summarizes every outpatient clinic handoff so tasks stop getting lost. Help me get to a useful first version quickly.

We cannot integrate with the electronic health record during the pilot. A clinic manager can spend thirty minutes per day running a manual test, and patient-identifying information must stay out of the prototype.

New evidence for this hypothetical benchmark: USER_PROVIDED observation notes from three de-identified handoff walkthroughs show that missing summaries were not the main breakdown. Staff usually knew the task, but ownership changed silently when schedules shifted; two tasks were duplicated because both teams acted. One walkthrough still included a genuinely missing detail. These are illustrative supplied notes, not verified clinical research. What do you change?

Use the complete trajectory to revise the problem frame, assumptions, and next move. Preserve the missing-information possibility without averaging away the ownership evidence. Choose one privacy-safe test that maximizes what we learn before integration work.

rubric_focus: Explores information, ownership, coordination, and recovery frames rather than equating the problem with summarization.
Honors privacy and integration constraints while proposing a realistic manual experiment.
Moves backward to reframing when supplied observations contradict the initial solution and preserves the missing-detail outlier.
Selects a test whose observable signals distinguish ownership visibility from summary quality.
